item.title: Prevalence and Characteristics of Coma in Latin American Critical Care Units: The COMA LATAM Study
item.description:
Objectives: To determine the point prevalence of coma across Latin American critical care units, characterize its etiology, and explore short-term outcomes.

Design: Multinational, cross-sectional point prevalence study with exploratory 14-day follow-up assessment.

Setting: Three hundred ninety-two hospitals across 19 Latin American countries, including ICUs, intermediate care units, neurocritical care units, cardiovascular ICUs, and trauma ICUs.

Patients: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) meeting the Coma Epidemiology, Evaluation, and Therapy care survey (COME-TOGETHER) criteria on May 28, 2024. Patients under deep sedation or pharmacological coma induction were excluded unless the coma state preceded pharmacological intervention.

Interventions: None (observational study).

Measurements and main results: Among 8305 critically ill patients, 1145 met coma criteria (point prevalence 13.8%), with country-specific rates ranging from 5.1% to 36.8%. Individual patient data were available for 729 patients (63.7%). Traumatic brain injury was the leading individual cause (24.8%), followed by hypoxic-anoxic brain injury (14.6%) and intracerebral hemorrhage (13.5%). When categorized by pathophysiology, vascular causes predominated (48.6%), followed by traumatic brain injury (24.8%) and other causes (26.6%). Age-stratified analysis revealed trauma predominantly affecting younger patients, while cerebrovascular causes predominated in older groups. Among patients with 14-day follow-up data (29% of cohort), mortality was 29.2%, with 67.7% of survivors recovering from coma. Only the Charlson Comorbidity Index was independently associated with implementation of life-sustaining therapy limitations (adjusted odds ratio, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.15-1.30; p < 0.001).

Conclusions: Coma affects nearly one in seven ICU beds across Latin America, with substantial country variation and distinct age-dependent etiology patterns. The significant burden highlights the need for targeted prevention strategies and specialized neurocritical care resources throughout the region.

Giglio A, Reccius A, Ferre A, Pino M, Carvajal C, Ciarrochi N

item.title: ICU Mortality Associated With Clinically Important Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Multistate Analysis
item.description:
Objectives: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding may increase mortality and time to discharge from the ICU. Conventional analyses ignore timing and treat bleeding as a binary event. We evaluated the association between time-dependent clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding and ICU mortality.

Design and setting: A multicenter cohort study using data from an international stress ulcer prophylaxis trial.

Patients: A total of 4821 invasively ventilated adult participants.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: A multistate model was specified with two transient ICU states (bleed-free and post-bleed) and four absorbing states (ICU discharge or death, each with or without bleeding). The Aalen-Johansen method was used to estimate transition and state occupancy probabilities and to describe risks of different clinical courses. Follow-up was censored at 90 days. We fit two Cox models for time to death in the ICU regressing on time-dependent bleeding history while adjusting for age, sex, baseline Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score, admission category (medical/surgical/trauma), vasopressor/inotrope use and renal replacement therapy on study day 1 and randomized allocation of pantoprazole or placebo; a second model also adjusted for time-dependent covariates of advanced life support (invasive mechanical ventilation, vasopressor/inotrope use, and renal replacement therapy). Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding developed in 104 patients (2.2%) in the ICU. Median ICU length of stay for those who experienced bleeding was 19 days (interquartile range [IQR], 11-30 d) vs. 9 days (IQR, 5-15 d) for those who did not. Accounting for immortal time bias, the time-dependent indicator of clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding was associated with increased ICU mortality (hazard ratio, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.13-2.15). At any time, patients who experienced bleeding had approximately 1.6 times the hazard of ICU mortality compared with those without a history of bleeding.

Conclusions: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding as a time-dependent event is associated with an increased risk of ICU mortality.

Wang Y, Heels-Ansdell D, Parpia S, Cook D, Kuriyama A, Guyatt G

item.title: Age-Related Differences in the Organ Donation Process Among Pediatric Brain-Dead Donors: A Nationwide Study in Japan
item.description:
Objectives: To characterize the pediatric organ donation process and age-related differences among brain-dead donors in Japan and evaluate organ-specific transplantation rates and graft survival across age groups.

Design: Nationwide retrospective cohort study.

Setting: National donor records maintained by the Japan Organ Transplant Network.

Patients: All pediatric (≤ 17 yr old) brain-dead organ donors in Japan between July 17, 2010, and March 31, 2024.

Interventions: None.

Measurement and main results: A total of 100 pediatric brain-dead organ donors were included. Donors were categorized into three age groups: younger than 6 years (n = 32), 6-14 years (n = 48), and 15-17 years (n = 20). The time intervals from hospital admission to organ procurement showed marked age-dependent prolongation, with median durations of 28, 19.5, and 13.5 days, respectively (p < 0.01). Younger donors were more frequently managed in children's hospitals and pediatric departments, whereas older donors were increasingly managed in emergency and critical care settings. Organ transplantation was achieved in 99% of donors. Organ-specific transplantation rates were consistently high for the heart, liver, and kidneys across all age groups, whereas lung and pancreas transplantation rates increased with donor age. During donor management, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic function were generally maintained or improved until procurement. No significant age-related differences in graft survival were observed for any organ type.

Conclusions: The pediatric organ donation process in Japan was substantially prolonged in an age-dependent manner, particularly among donors younger than 6 years. Despite prolonged donor management, transplantation rates remained high, and no significant age-related differences in graft survival were observed. These findings highlight the importance of sustained multidisciplinary and family support throughout the donation process and may provide insights for pediatric donation systems in low-volume settings.

Obara T, Tsukahara K, Nojima T, Hiraoka T, Morikawa T, Ueda Y

item.title: High-Flow Nasal Cannula Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adults With De Novo Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis
item.description:
Objectives: To evaluate the efficacy of high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) compared with conventional oxygen therapy (COT) in adults with de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) using a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA).

Data sources: MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception to April 7, 2026.

Study selection: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing HFNC with COT in adults with de novo AHRF.

Data extraction: Two investigators independently performed study selection, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and certainty assessment, with discrepancies resolved through discussion.

Data synthesis: A total of 13 RCTs involving 4294 patients were included in the analysis. Compared with COT, HFNC was associated with a lower risk of intubation (Risk ratio [RR], 0.88; 95% CI, 0.78-0.99; low certainty), but not mortality (RR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.83-1.10; moderate certainty). TSA indicated that the cumulative evidence was insufficient to establish a conclusive effect for either outcome. Although HFNC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in hospital length of stay (mean difference, -0.84 d; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.43; low certainty), the clinical importance of this reduction remains uncertain. No significant differences were observed in escalation of therapy (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.75-1.01; very low certainty), ICU admission (RR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.50-1.39; very low certainty), or ICU length of stay (mean difference, -0.10 d; 95% CI, -0.82 to 0.61; very low certainty).

Conclusions: In adults with de novo AHRF, HFNC may reduce the need for endotracheal intubation but probably does not improve survival compared with COT.

Lin P, Li X, Wang Y, Liang Z, Wang T

item.title: The Radiographic Lung Edema Score in Pediatric Acute Respiratory Failure: Associations With Systemic Inflammatory Biomarkers and Multiple Organ Dysfunction
item.description:
Objectives: Although chest radiographs (CXR) are among the most used imaging modalities in critically ill patients, their interpretation and clinical significance remain incompletely leveraged. The Radiographic Lung Edema (RALE) score is a prognostic bedside tool widely applied in adults to quantify lung edema on CXR. However, this score has been infrequently studied in children, and its potential to reflect broader aspects of critical illness pathophysiology beyond the lungs is unknown. We sought to determine the reproducibility of the RALE score, and whether higher RALE scores were associated with circulating inflammatory and endothelial biomarkers, multi-organ dysfunction, and worse clinical outcomes in pediatric acute respiratory failure (ARF).

Design: Retrospective cohort study.

Setting: Multicenter PICUs.

Patients: Critically ill children (2 wk to 17 yr old) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for ARF, enrolled in the CAF-PINT (Coagulation and Fibrinolysis in Pediatric Insulin Titration) study (2012-2016).

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: A baseline RALE score was calculated for each patient from a single CXR obtained within 72 hours of IMV initiation. Among 212 patients, RALE scores demonstrated good inter-rater reliability (intra-class coefficient 0.85; 95% CI, 0.82-0.87). After adjustment for ARF etiology and illness severity, higher RALE scores were associated with fewer 28-day ventilator-free days (sub-distribution hazard ratio per 1-sd increase, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95). Structural equation modeling demonstrated that this association was mediated through both pulmonary dysfunction, measured by the oxygenation index (β -0.14; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.22 to -0.06), and extrapulmonary organ dysfunction, measured by the Pediatric Logistic Organ Dysfunction score (β -0.05; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.10 to -0.002). Similar associations were observed for 28-day PICU-free days. Finally, penalized regression selected soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, and tumor necrosis factor receptor-1 as biomarkers associated with higher RALE scores.

Conclusions: We provide evidence that the RALE score is not solely a lung injury marker but also reflects broader systemic pathophysiology. These findings have important implications for the interpretation and clinical application of this bedside tool in pediatric ARF.

Sallee CJ, Whitney JE, Markovic D, Zinter MS, Do N, Lim MJ

item.title: Religion and Religiosity in End-of-Life Decisions in Neurocritical Care
item.description:
Objectives: End-of-life decisions are shaped by diverse biographical, social, and cultural factors. Few studies have systematically examined the impact of religion on end-of-life decisions, and even less data are available on religiosity (i.e., strength of religious faith). The Religion and religiosity in End-of-life deCisiOns in neuroCritIcaL carE (RECONCILE) study aimed to investigate whether religiosity, rather than religion, plays a decisive role in shaping end-of-life decisions.

Design: Prospective observational study.

Setting: The study was conducted between 2021 and 2024 at two neuro-ICUs at Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin.

Patients: We prospectively studied patients with acute brain injury and poor neurologic prognosis defined by the absence of regaining decision-making capacity or sufficient autonomy. A total of 100 patients were included.

Interventions: None.

Measurements: Relatives were consulted to ascertain the patients' presumed wishes regarding the continuation or withdrawal of life-sustaining intensive care. The 10-item Santa Clara Strength of Religious Faith questionnaire was applied to measure the patient´s religiosity on a scale between 10 and 40 points. We applied the t-test for independent variables to evaluate the influence of religiosity on end-of-life decisions. To adjust for possible confounders like age, sex, nationality, and religion, we calculated a logistic regression as well as an analysis of variance calculation.

Main results: In patients in whom intensive care was continued, the median score was significantly higher compared with patients in whom intensive care was withdrawn (28.1 ± 9.0 vs. 20.5 ± 8.3; p < 0.001; Cohens d = 0.875). This finding was reproduced in each denominational group. Religion, age, and sex showed no significant association with the end-of-life decision behavior. Germans chose withdrawal of therapy significantly more often than non-Germans (p = 0.01) but also showed significantly lower religiosity scores (21.9 vs. 27.9; p = 0.003).

Conclusions: The RECONCILE study demonstrates that religiosity looks more important in influencing end-of-life decisions than religion. Higher levels of religiosity were associated with a preference for more aggressive treatment, even when neurologic prognosis is poor.

Tempel HM, Wolf S, Salih F

item.title: A Guytonian Atlas of Venous Return in Septic Shock: Reconstruction of Hemodynamic States
item.description:
Objectives: To reconstruct venous return physiology across published studies of septic shock and characterize the distribution of circulatory states represented in the literature.

Design: Exploratory physiologic reconstruction study.

Setting: Secondary analysis of published hemodynamic observations.

Patients: Adult patients with septic shock reported in studies containing sufficient information for reconstruction of mean circulatory filling pressure analogue (Pmca) and related parameters including venous return driving pressure (VRdP) and resistance to venous return (RVR).

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: A total of 150 observations were available. Median Pmca, central venous pressure (CVP), VRdP, and RVR were 17.3 mm Hg, 9.0 mm Hg, 7.9 mm Hg, and 1.04 mm Hg/min/L, respectively. Empirical quartiles identified four recurrent circulatory phenotypes: reduced filling pressure/gradient, preserved venous return, elevated venous pressure, and high-resistance venous return. The preserved venous return pattern demonstrated the highest median cardiac output (CO), whereas the high-resistance pattern exhibited the lowest flow despite comparable filling pressures. In exploratory adjusted analyses incorporating available vasopressor exposure and fluid-therapy context, VRdP remained strongly associated with CO (β, 1.03 L/min/mm Hg; 95% CI, 0.80-1.25; p < 0.001). When Pmca and CVP were entered separately, Pmca was positively associated with CO (β, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.79-1.25; p < 0.001), whereas CVP was inversely associated with CO (β, -1.03; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.80; p < 0.001).

Conclusions: Published hemodynamic observations in septic shock occupy distinct Guytonian phenotypes characterized by different combinations of circulatory filling pressure, venous pressure, and RVR. Reconstruction of venous return geometry may provide a physiologic framework for interpreting circulatory heterogeneity in septic shock.

Chalkias A, Mavridis T, Papagiannakis N, Katsifa K, Nikolaidis I, Laou E

item.title: Association of Care Intensity With Survival and Long-Term Cost-Effectiveness in Sepsis Without Initial Organ Support After Emergency Admission: A Multicenter Cohort Study in Japan
item.description:
Objectives: To identify subgroups of patients hospitalized for community-acquired sepsis without initial organ support who may derive survival and cost-effectiveness benefits from ICU or high-dependency care unit (HDU) admission.

Design: Retrospective cohort study.

Setting: A 140-hospital Japanese database (April 2016-March 2024).

Patients: Adults admitted via emergency ambulance for community-acquired sepsis not requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, mechanical ventilation, catecholamines, or renal replacement therapy before or on the antimicrobial-initiation day.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: We compared ICU and HDU admissions, each vs. general ward (GW) admission, balancing patient characteristics using overlap propensity-score weighting. In-hospital mortality was estimated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs using modified Poisson regression. Cost-effectiveness was measured by the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in 3-year costs per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among 28,211 patients (GW, 18,349; HDU, 8,706; ICU, 1,156), ICU and HDU admissions were not associated with lower mortality overall (HDU vs. GW; RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.92-1.06 and ICU vs. GW; RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.92-1.22). However, HDU admission was associated with lower mortality among patients with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score greater than or equal to 6 (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.99) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score less than or equal to 12 (RR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.71-0.92). Under the Japanese (50,000 USD/QALY) and U.S. (100,000 USD/QALY) thresholds, ICU and HDU admissions were not cost-effective overall (ICERs > 200,000 USD/QALY). However, the HDU subgroup with GCS score less than or equal to 12 (ICER, 47,738 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 45,918-49,558) was cost-effective under both thresholds, and that with SOFA score greater than or equal to 6 (ICER, 55,319 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 52,018-58,624) met the U.S. threshold.

Conclusions: ICU or HDU admission was not associated with survival or economic benefits overall, whereas HDU subgroups (SOFA score ≥ 6 or GCS score ≤ 12) were associated with lower mortality and better cost-effectiveness. These findings may help optimize resource allocation.

Hashimoto Y, Inoue N, Yoshida M, Iketani R, Imai S
